- wingcomm · comment · 2026-07-02T16:19:56Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4867894431)

@aligningmyself's `persistent_topk` finding looks like a direct hit on our wedge — we're the long-context real-traffic case of exactly that failure.

**Our config sits inside the (384k, 512k) ceiling.** We run `max_model_len=524288` on 4× GB10 (TP=4/EP=4), serving Hermes. Live prompt-length histogram right now: of ~70 substantive requests (excluding ping/monitoring traffic), **~34 (≈49%) are in the 200K–500K band** — Hermes is a heavy long-context user, so a large fraction of real requests are near or above the `total_ctas > num_sms*occupancy=48` crossover.

**Incidents 14/15/16 line up with `persistent_topk` oversubscription as the *cause*, with cudagraph as the *manifestation*:**
- Same suspect you named (#2, the lightning-indexer top-k, no timeout).
- The MTBF fits: we wedge every ~16–45h — i.e. when a request happens to accumulate past ~400k context, not on every large request.
- **Hang vs. error:** @aligningmyself hit a catchable `RuntimeError` under **enforce-eager**; we're on **FULL cudagraph**, where the oversubscribed launch is inside a captured/replayed graph and can't fail gracefully — so it **silently wedges** instead. That also explains our py-spy victim frames (`_forward_prefill`, then `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang` ×2): the indexer kernel stalls the stream, and py-spy catches whatever op tries to launch next — consistent with the victim-vs-culprit reframe.

**On the PIECEWISE experiment:** we flipped to `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE` before this finding. If the cause is `persistent_topk` oversubscription it won't *fix* the wedge (same kernel) — but it may convert our silent hang into aligningmyself's catchable `RuntimeError`, which would itself confirm the mechanism. We'll keep it running and report which we get.

**What we can do that @aligningmyself's rig can't:** we're a **different topology (4-node TP=4/EP=4, RoCE)** under **real long-context production traffic**, so we're a second independent repro. Two offers:

@wingcomm @aligningmyself — your combined diagnosis is right, and there's now a fix landed on this PR branch (`codex/ds4-sm120-min-enable`, commit `9bccfd1388`).

**Confirming the unification.** I reproduced and root-caused it on our GB10:
- `persistent_topk`'s cooperative-radix "large" path (seq_len > 32768) needs all `ctas_per_group` CTAs **co-resident** for a spin-wait barrier. `ctas_per_group` grows with context; past `num_sms*occupancy` (48 on GB10) it can't fit and falls back to `FilteredTopK`, which requires ≥128 KB smem/block — GB10 exposes only ~99 KB → the hard fail. Pinned the exact knee with a standalone sweep: clean ≤384k, `total_ctas=49 > 48` at 400k (deterministic, kernel-bound; independent of the top-k value — it's stride/context-width driven).
- @wingcomm's **hang-vs-error** reframe is exactly it: under `--enforce-eager` the oversubscribed launch throws a catchable `RuntimeError` (aligningmyself); under FULL cudagraph the same launch is inside a captured/replayed graph and **can't fail gracefully → silent wedge**. Same culprit, and the indexer stall is why py-spy catches whatever op launches next (`mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`) — victim, not culprit.

**The fix (`9bccfd1388`).** Gate on smem **capacity** (`max_smem_per_block < 128 KB`), not capability family (RTX 50-series is also family-120 with ~100 KB). On those parts: force `ctas_per_group=1` + `needs_cooperative=false` — no cooperative barrier at all — and route long rows to a new **exact single-CTA streaming radix** (`histogram_streaming_topk`): a 4-round MSD radix that re-streams the row from global each round (filtered by the accumulated prefix) plus a streaming collection. This removes **both** failure modes at once:
- the oversubscribe hard-fail (no co-residency requirement), and
- the cooperative spin-wait barrier that deadlocks under a captured NCCL collective — it's simply never executed on these parts, which should address the silent wedge directly.

Two things I deliberately did **not** do, and why:
- **Not** a smem-shrunk `FilteredTopK` — it still buffers equal-to-threshold candidates in a bounded list; I measured the analogous buffer (`histogram_256_topk`'s `MAX_BUFFERED_ITEMS`) **overflow and under-select at dense long-context pivots** (74/2048 wrong at 256k), so a shrunk fallback would be approximate.
- **Not** GB10-aware tiling of the cooperative path — it keeps the barrier, so it wouldn't remove the FULL-cudagraph hang mechanism.

The streaming path never buffers, so it's exact and barrier-free. `≥128 KB` devices (Hopper, datacenter Blackwell) are byte-identical — all changes are behind the smem gate.

**Validated on our GB10 (2-node TP=2):**
- Kernel **bit-exact vs `torch.topk`** and vs the cooperative path across 128k–640k context, topk 512/2048, multi-row (the cases the buffered path got wrong are now exact).
- Served DeepSeek-V4-Flash at `max_model_len=524288` on **FULL_AND_PIECEWISE cudagraph** — came up healthy (the sparse-MLA warmup dummy-run at ~524k width, which hard-fails pre-fix, now passes), needle-recall at ~434k = 2/2, coherent, no oversubscribe/Xid.

**Please take you up on the 4-node test.** Our validation is 2-node TP=2; your **4-node TP=4/EP=4 under real long-context Hermes traffic on FULL cudagraph** is the ideal confirmation, especially across an MTBF window — if the silent wedge stops recurring on `9bccfd1388`, that's the smoking-gun on the hang side that our short 2-node window can't show. @aligningmyself — likewise for the 1M case on your 6× GB10 (and I can share the needle-recall harness you asked for). The all-rank capture is still worth having if it wedges again, but I'd hope it won't.

The default (relaxed-ordering on) routes CUDA-buffer registration through `ibv_reg_mr_iova2`, which faceplants on the unified memory and degrades to socket — so you think you're on RDMA and you're not. - GanyX19 · comment · 2026-07-03T11:09:52Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4875536713)

### Two findings on the sm12x DeepSeek-V4 path (host-memory leak + a perf regression), from running this branch on GB10 / DGX Spark (sm_121)

Sharing two related issues found while running this branch under sustained load on GB10 unified-memory hardware, both in `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/ops/`. Happy to open a PR against this branch if useful.

---

#### 1. Unbounded per-shape Triton recompilation in the MQA-logits kernels → host-memory leak → hard freeze

The three `@triton.jit` kernels in `sm12x_mqa.py` — `_fp8_mqa_logits_kernel`, `_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_kernel`, `_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_rowwise_kernel` — declare per-request-varying values as `tl.constexpr`:

- `num_rows` / `num_q`
- `logits_width` / `seq_len_kv` ( = `token_count`, the KV/context length)
- `stride_lm` ( = the logits row stride, also `token_count`)

Triton compiles and **caches a distinct kernel per distinct value**, retained for the process lifetime. Instrumenting `CompiledKernel.__init__` and counting distinct compile signatures, `_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_rowwise_kernel` shows **distinct == total (100 % compile-cache miss)** — a fresh kernel per call. On GB10 the compile cache lives in the same unified memory as the model, so it grows unbounded (~5–6 GB/h/node under production-like load, freed only by an engine restart) until the host hard-freezes.

These values are used **only** in runtime boundary masks (`offs < num_rows`, `offs < logits_width`) and address arithmetic (`* stride_lm`) — never as a `tl.arange` extent or a `range()`/`tl.range()` loop bound (those are the separate `BLOCK_*` / `num_heads` / `head_dim` constexprs). So they can be plain runtime scalars; Triton then specializes at most on divisibility (~2–4 variants total). After the change the kernel drops out of the top recompilers and host-memory growth under the same load goes to ≈ 0; output and throughput are unchanged.

```diff
@@ _fp8_paged_mqa_logits_rowwise_kernel / _fp8_paged_mqa_logits_kernel / _fp8_mqa_logits_kernel @@
-    num_rows: tl.constexpr,
-    logits_width: tl.constexpr,
+    num_rows,
+    logits_width,
...
-    stride_lm: tl.constexpr,
+    stride_lm,
```
(9 signature lines across the 3 kernels; no call-site changes — the same ints are already passed.) `stride_ln` (=1) and all tile/shape constexprs stay as-is.

---

#### 2. `_deepseek_v4_sm12x_fp8_einsum_kernel` is already runtime here — but missing an alignment hint, which costs ~24 % single-stream decode

This branch already declares `num_tokens`, `a_stride_group`, `a_scale_stride_group` as runtime in `fp8_einsum.py` (good — that avoids the same leak there). But there is **no `tl.multiple_of` hint**, and that turns out to cost real throughput: `a_stride_group` is the A-tile stride used in the hot loop right before `tl.dot`, and as a plain runtime scalar Triton drops it to divisibility=1 and narrows the load.

Bisection on a pinned build, single-stream decode (temp 0, MTP-2, 256K, idle):

| build | tok/s |
|---|---|
| baseline (MQA still constexpr) | 38.4 |
| + MQA fix from §1 only | 38.2 (free) |
| + sibling args runtime (this branch's einsum state) | **29.2 (−24 %)** |
| + the two hints below | **39.0 (recovered)** |

Recovery keeps the values runtime (no leak reintroduced), at the top of the kernel body:

```python
a_stride_group       = tl.multiple_of(a_stride_group, 16)        # = num_tokens * hidden_size, hidden_size % 128 == 0
a_scale_stride_group = tl.multiple_of(a_scale_stride_group, 16)  # = num_tokens * 32
```

Both are provably ÷16. I did **not** hint `stride_lm` (raw context length), `a_scale_stride_hidden`, or the tf32 `stride_outs` (=`m·24`) / `stride_sqs` — those aren't provably ÷16 and a false `multiple_of` would corrupt memory; they're store/scale paths and negligible anyway.

---

#### 3. Minor: `_tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm_kernel`
`stride_outs` / `stride_sqs` are still `constexpr` and vary with `M` — same per-shape recompile pattern (small contributor, only material at 1M context). Same constexpr→runtime treatment; no hint needed (store path, not ÷16-provable).

Measurements are from one GB10/sm_121 TP=2 setup; numbers will vary, but the mechanism (constexpr compile-cache on unified memory) and the `multiple_of` recovery should be general. Glad to send a PR if you'd like.

- jasl · comment · 2026-07-04T11:07:49Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4881740564)

@wingcomm — this is fantastic to hear, thank you for the production confirmation. 11h+ at full 1M with zero wedges, the 1M cudagraph warmup capturing clean, and the ~5–6 GB/h → ~1.9 MB/h memory-creep cut (~3000×, "the 17h-restart treadmill is over") are exactly the outcomes we were hoping for — and the KV-pool bonus at 1M (4.63M vs 2.91M @512K from the C128A workspace self-sizing) is a nice surprise. Really appreciate you closing the loop with hard numbers on a real EP=4 rig.

On the long-context prefill monopolization — good diagnosis, and your read is mostly right. Answers:

**1. Is the streaming-radix cost inherent to 99 KB smem? — No, it's a conservative floor, and there's real headroom.**
The `histogram_streaming_topk` path re-streams the row from global on each of its 4 MSD-radix rounds — that's ~4× full-row reads at 1M, which is the cost you're seeing. We shipped it that way for *exactness* under the 99 KB cap (the bounded-buffer `histogram_256` path under-selects at dense pivots — >4096 ties in a 256-bin threshold bin — which is why it's gated to ≤32 KB-context). But it doesn't have to re-read the *whole* row every round:
- After round 1 you already know the top 8-bit bin; rounds 2–4 only need the elements *in* that bin (~N/256), which for 1M is ~4096 — small enough to buffer in smem. So a "narrow-after-round-1" variant is ~1 full read + 3 passes over a few-K buffer, not 4 full reads.
- Even simpler: our own `histogram_2048` (2048-bin, single-pass + bounded buffer) fits 99 KB and at 1M has only ~488 elements per threshold bin — well under the 4096 buffer, so it *wouldn't* overflow. It's currently capped at `HIST2048_THRESHOLD=8192` conservatively; extending a finer single-pass histogram to the long-context force_noncooperative path (with the 4-round re-stream kept only as the rare genuinely-dense fallback) should recover most of the cost.

So: the re-stream is exact-and-safe, not minimal. I think it's optimizable and I'd like to prototype the finer-histogram/narrow variant — **your sweep offer is exactly what would guide it** (see below).

**2. Scheduling lever — the reason chunked-prefill barely helped is structural, and it bounds the fix.**
The indexer top-k is over the **accumulated** context, not the query chunk. So splitting a 1M prefill into chunks doesn't split the top-k work — each late-context chunk still runs a ~full-context top-k (the ~seconds you measured), it just reschedules it. Smaller `max_num_batched_tokens` interleaves finer but every late chunk is still heavy, so you hit a floor. The levers that *do* help are the partial-prefill ones, not the batched-token size: set `max_num_partial_prefills > 1` and a `long_prefill_token_threshold` below your prompt size — that classifies the 1M prefill as "long" and lets short prompts **jump ahead** between its chunks (`max_long_partial_prefills` caps how many long ones run concurrently). That bounds the *starvation* (your Waiting 0→4 backing up) even though it can't shrink the long prefill's own cost. It's a latency-for-small-requests win, not a throughput win — the throughput fix is making the top-k cheaper (#1).

**3. Is more of the prefill recoverable like the einsum? — No, different kind of floor.**
The einsum win was a Triton *alignment* recovery (`tl.multiple_of`) — narrowed loads, free to restore. The top-k cost is algorithmic/bandwidth (the re-stream), so an alignment hint won't touch it; the recoverable part there is #1 (finer histogram). It's worth auditing the other long-context prefill kernels (sparse-MLA prefill, the MoE GEMMs) for their own alignment/warmup recoveries, but the top-k is the algorithmic hard part at 1M — and, as you note, decode being NCCL-spin-wait-bound on this fabric means you can't hide the prefill behind other work, which compounds it independently of the kernel.

**On the sweep — yes please.** A controlled prefill-latency-vs-context sweep on your 4-node 1M/EP=4 rig would be genuinely useful: it'd confirm whether the top-k actually dominates the step (vs the sparse-MLA prefill / MoE) at 1M, and give me a target curve to validate a finer-histogram prototype against. If you can capture per-context-length step time (say 128K / 256K / 512K / 1M, single large prefill, idle otherwise) plus a py-spy/nsys sample of where the ~110s goes, that pins it. If the top-k is the bulk, I'll take a run at the finer-histogram variant and send you a patch to try. We don't have a 4-node/1M setup here (our GB10 validation is 2-node), so your rig is the real characterization platform.

@wingcomm — didn't wait for the sweep: took a run at the finer-histogram top-k and it's landed on this branch (`codex/ds4-sm120-min-enable`, `9f18be7630`), ready for you to try.

**What it is.** The 4-round streaming radix re-read the full row 4× (once per MSD-radix round). The new path (`histogram_2048_topk<TopK, CacheBins=false>` in `persistent_topk.cuh`) does the finer-histogram approach we discussed: Phase 1 builds the 2048-bin histogram, Phase 2 re-reads once and collects, Phase 3 exactly refines the buffered pivot bin. **2 full-row reads instead of 4.** The finer bins keep the pivot bin small (~seq/2048 ≈ 488 at 1M, well under the 3708 tie buffer), so it stays single-CTA / 99 KB-smem-safe. If the pivot bin *does* overflow (fp16 bins clustering — e.g. thousands of exactly-equal logits), it falls back to the streaming radix, so it's provably exact for any distribution.

**Validated (GB10 2-node here):**
- Bit-exact vs `torch.topk` across 64K–1M × {spread, dense-pivot, >4096-exact-ties} — value multiset identical, no dups, fallback verified.
- Kernel time (single row): 64K 0.038 vs 0.059 ms, 256K 0.078 vs 0.159, 512K 0.128 vs 0.291, **1M 0.229 vs 0.557 ms — 2.43×**. The win grows with context (it's read-bound, so halving reads pays off more the longer the row). Only the rare overflow/dense-pivot case is ~12% slower (5 reads: the histogram pass + the streaming fallback).
- Serve: DSv4-Flash at `max_model_len=524288`, arthur needle-recall at ~434K = 2/2, clean, no oversubscribe/errors — the 2-pass path is correct in the real indexer.

**The honest caveat, and where your sweep comes in.** This is 2.4× on the *top-k*. Whether it moves your ~110 s prefill depends on how much of that step the top-k actually is — which is exactly what your prefill-latency-vs-context sweep + a py-spy/nsys sample would show. If the top-k dominates, you should see a real cut; if the sparse-MLA prefill / MoE dominate, less so (and those are the next targets). - wingcomm · comment · 2026-07-05T01:00:41Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4884342262)

Problem definition: long-context prefill is slow on GB10 (4-node TP=4/EP=4, 1M ctx)

## The root: a single large prefill is minutes long — no concurrency involved

One request, ~536K prompt tokens, `max_tokens=1`, engine otherwise light: **prefill (TTFT) = 573 s (~9.5 min).** ≈930 tok/s prefill. That's a single request — no parallelism, no scheduler contention — so it isolates the raw kernel cost cleanly. It lines up with your own 2-node number (535K needle = 513 s), so it reproduces across topology.

This is the problem. Everything else is a consequence of it.

## Where the ~9.5 min goes

py-spy sampling the worker's MainThread across the prefill (8 samples):

| component | share |
|---|---:|
| sparse-MLA attention (`flashmla` / `attention_impl`) | ~50% |
| MoE (`fused_moe`) | ~37% |
| indexer / top-k (`sparse_attn_indexer`) | ~12% |

So your `histogram_2048` top-k win (2.43× on ~12% of the step) is a real ~7–15% per-prefill cut — but **the sparse-MLA attention (~50%) and MoE (~37%) dominate long-context prefill**, and look like the higher-leverage targets. The step is also interconnect-latency-bound here (GPUs spin-wait on NCCL over the CX7 fabric), so launch-overhead reductions mostly don't help — it's genuinely kernel/comms time.

**Profile caveat:** this is py-spy (samples where the Python thread sits — often parked in a `cuLaunchKernel`), a proxy for GPU time, not a kernel timeline. nsys isn't in the serving container and host-attach needs sudo we don't have on these nodes — so if a real nsys/ncu GPU-kernel breakdown would sharpen the MLA-vs-MoE split, we'll relaunch the serve under nsys in a maintenance window and capture a 1M-prefill trace. Say the word.

## Why it surfaces as a "stall with parallel requests"

The several-minute single-prefill is the cost the submitter of a big request pays. It becomes a *stall for everyone else* under concurrency because `max_num_partial_prefills=1` (default) → the engine prefills **one request at a time**, so N concurrent large requests serialize:
```
07:31:55  prompt 0.0 tok/s  gen 0.0  Running 2  Waiting 0   <- one prefill monopolizes
07:33:15  prompt 0.0 tok/s  gen 0.3  Running 2  Waiting 4   <- queue backs up ~110s
07:33:55  prompt 11609 tok/s gen 51  Running 3  Waiting 1   <- prefill lands, recovers
```
So **parallel-stall ≈ N × single-prefill-time.** Chunked prefill doesn't hide it — the indexer top-k is over the *accumulated* context, so every late chunk still does ~full-context work.

## Fix space
- **Kernel (yours, the root):** MLA-attention + MoE dominate the ~9.5-min prefill — bigger targets than the top-k for long-context latency. Speeding these helps single-request TTFT *and* the parallel stall equally.
- **Scheduler (ours):** `max_num_partial_prefills` gates the serialization; raising it *might* overlap prefills, but with the accumulated-context top-k + interconnect-bound step our guess is it'd thrash — an open question we'd value your read on.

- jasl · comment · 2026-07-05T10:38:57Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4885707471)

This is excellent isolation work — thank you. It matches our read, and it correctly reframes where the top-k sits.

**Agreed on the shape.** top-k ≈12%, and your ~7–15%-per-prefill math for the 2-pass histogram is right — it was always aimed at the top-k *monopolization* (the 4-read streaming blowup when a ~1M-context row overflows the register cache), never the prefill floor. MLA + MoE are the floor, and it's interconnect-bound — that lines up with our own 2-node decode teardown (MoE-GEMM + NCCL-AR + dense-GEMM as the top-3), just shifted toward attention on the prefill side.

**One caveat before we chase the 50/37 split — py-spy will over-attribute to whichever kernel the NCCL-wait parks in.** On an interconnect-bound step the MainThread sits in `cuLaunchKernel` behind the collective, so a sample lands on whatever kernel is launching when the stall hits — which inflates the two biggest launchers (MLA + MoE) with comms-wait time. Your own caveat, and it's the load-bearing one: if a meaningful slice of the wall-clock is actually NCCL-wait overlapped onto those launches, the *true* GPU-kernel split — and therefore the target — moves. So **yes, please grab the nsys trace.** A single-request 536K (or 1M) prefill, `max_tokens=1`, GPU-kernel timeline is exactly what decides MLA-attn vs MoE-GEMM vs indexer vs comms. That's the gating measurement before either of us commits kernel effort — say the word and we'll take whatever you capture.

One thing already pointing that way: your 4-node **573s** is actually a hair *slower* than the 2-node **513s** for the same ~535K — i.e. adding two nodes bought more collective latency than compute relief. For a single fat prefill that's a fingerprint of the comms-bound regime (the fabric, not FLOPs, is the near-term wall), and it says the node count that minimizes single-prefill TTFT may be the *smallest* one that still holds the KV — the extra nodes are there for 1M capacity, not speed.

**One structural note that the trace should confirm:** the ~50% "sparse-MLA attention" in *prefill* is DSv4's MHA-style prefill path — a **different kernel from the sparse-*decode* one** the top-k / FI-SM120 work touches (the SM120 sparse backend is decode-only). So it's separately optimizable and, as you say, the higher-leverage target. On the MoE side (~37%), consumer-Blackwell defaults to Marlin W4A16; whether Marlin is the right kernel for these large prefill row-counts (vs a grouped-GEMM path) is an open question, and the natural large-batch MoE lever — DeepGEMM W4A8 — is currently blocked on SM120, so near-term it's Marlin or bust there. Since the step is comms-bound, the one no-rebuild knob worth a cheap A/B is NCCL tuning (algo/proto/channels for the fabric) — it won't touch kernel time but can shave the collective floor.

**On `max_num_partial_prefills` — your thrash instinct is right, for throughput.** A single 536K prefill already saturates both the GPU and the fabric, so running two concurrently adds no compute and no bandwidth — it splits the same resource, each prefill runs ~2× slower, and total wall-clock is ~unchanged (worse once the accumulated-context top-k runs for both). p50 for the first submitter degrades, the tail stays flat; serialize-at-1 is actually protecting mean TTFT. What raising it *would* help is a different goal — fairness for small requests stuck behind a big prefill — and the better lever there is chunked-prefill interleaving + `long_prefill_token_threshold` to cap the big prefill's per-step budget so small requests slip between its chunks. The catch you already named applies: the indexer top-k is over accumulated context, so every late chunk still pays ~full-context indexer cost → chunking makes the big prefill itself slower while unblocking the small ones (a fairness-vs-big-prefill-throughput trade, tunable via the threshold). It doesn't move the single-prefill floor — only the kernel does, and that (as you noted) helps single-request TTFT and the parallel stall equally.

So: **nsys next.** A single-request 1M/536K prefill GPU timeline decides whether the effort goes to the prefill-MLA kernel, the MoE GEMM, or the comms floor — grab it whenever the maintenance window opens and we'll target from there.

> @epheien Thanks for the report.

After the rebase, xgrammar's DeepSeek V4 non-reasoning structural tag excluded `</think>`, so the scheduler treated that otherwise harmless extra close tag as a grammar violation and terminated the request.
> 
> I pushed a narrow fix in `531807c34bf73f6ef095f203486e12dadfbdadb2`: for DeepSeek V4 non-reasoning strict tool-calling only, allow a stray `</think>` while still rejecting `<think>` and leaving the reasoning-mode structural tag unchanged.
> 
> Verified with:
> 
> * `tests/tool_parsers/test_structural_tag_registry.py -q`
> * `tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv4_tool_parser.py tests/reasoning/test_deepseekv4_reasoning_parser.py -q`
> * an xgrammar matcher check for `.</think>` and `.</think><｜DSML｜tool_calls>\n`
> 
> Please rebuild/redeploy the latest PR head and retry. If it still reproduces, please share the launch args around `--tool-call-parser`, `--reasoning-parser`, `VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING`, and MTP/spec decode settings.


@jasl Following up on the strict tool-calling grammar thread above — we hit what looks like a *different* xgrammar termination on a branch head that already includes `531807c34`: with **MTP spec decode enabled**, named-`tool_choice` requests with thinking on intermittently 500.

**Setup**: 2× RTX PRO 6000 workstation (sm_120), TP=2, commit `616a5723ac`, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark`.
**Launch args**: `--kv-cache-dtype=fp8 --max-model-len=32768 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser=deepseek_v4 --reasoning-parser=deepseek_v4 --speculative-config={"method": "deepseek_mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}`. `VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING` unset.

**Symptom**: in a 42-request structured-extraction batch (~8k-token prompts, concurrency 10), 7/42 returned `500 Internal server error` (~38 s server-side), correlated with bursts of:

```
/project/cpp/grammar_matcher.cc:612: Warning: The matcher has terminated after accepting the stop token, but is trying to accept new token with id 128825.
```

Unlike the June report, the rejected ids vary per request (128825, 119061, 112434, 1, …) — it reads like draft tokens still being proposed after the matcher accepted the stop token, not a fixed stray tag.

**Triangulation** (same workload): MTP off + thinking on → 42/42 OK. MTP on + thinking off (`chat_template_kwargs`) → 42/42 OK (warnings still logged, requests succeed). MTP on + thinking on → 7/42 → 500. Not reproducible with a short single request — appears load/length-dependent.

Workaround we're shipping: thinking off whenever a function is forced via `tool_choice` (no exact-match loss on our extraction evals). Happy to provide full logs or test a patch. Otherwise the branch has been excellent on sm_120 — MTP alone takes us 85 → 151 tok/s single-stream.

---
*Disclosure: I'm not an expert in AI hardware or vLLM internals — this report was put together with extensive help from Claude Code. Numbers and logs are from real runs; the root-cause reading may be off, happy to be corrected.*

- jasl · comment · 2026-07-05T19:30:28Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4887327455)

@jedelacarrera Thank you — this was an excellent report, and your instinct was right on two counts: the workaround is sound, and the `grammar_matcher.cc … terminated` warning was a red herring (it fires in the passing case too).

**Reproduced** on a 2-node GB10 (TP=2) with your configuration — MTP + `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4`, thinking on, forced `tool_choice`, ~8k-token prompts @ concurrency 10: **16/42 → 500**. It's an upstream structured-output × spec-decode issue and is independent of hardware (the buggy code lives in the scheduler / structured-output manager), so it applies to your sm120 setup as well.

**Root cause** (not the terminated matcher): every 500 is `scheduler.py … Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens … Terminating request`, and the rejected token lists decode to the *reasoning tail + `</think>`* — e.g. `[270, 4105, 16, 128822]` = `" the tool.</think>"`. Under speculative decoding, when the reasoning stream ends **inside a single MTP step**, the scheduler was advancing the tool-call structural-tag grammar over the pre-`</think>` reasoning tokens; the grammar correctly rejects them and the request is terminated. That's exactly why it's thinking-on + MTP-on only: thinking-off has no reasoning tokens to mis-feed, and non-MTP never straddles the boundary within a single step.

This is already fixed upstream by **#44297** ("Constrain bitmask and trim grammar advance at the reasoning boundary"). I've **backported it** to this branch (`codex/ds4-sm120-min-enable` / `ds4-sm120-preview-dev`, commit `fe486bf6`). It's a pure-Python change — no kernel rebuild required.

**Validated** on the same box: the identical 42-request workload → **42/42, 0×500, 0 terminated requests**; and #44297's own test suite (`tests/v1/spec_decode/test_mtp_structured_output.py`, incl. `test_bitmask_constrained_when_reasoning_ends_midwindow`) passes on our hardware.

Please pull the latest branch head and retry. Your thinking-off-under-forced-`tool_choice` workaround is a perfectly good stopgap in the meantime. Thanks again — the decoded token ids and the MTP/thinking triangulation in your report made this quick to pin down.

One heads-up: after #44297 you may still see a few **non-fatal** `Failed to advance FSM … Please file an issue.` log lines under this workload — that's an expected, tolerated artifact of #44297's bitmask-simulation path (it probes post-reasoning drafts and tolerates rejection, but `accept_tokens` still logs). Requests succeed; it's cosmetic only.

- wingcomm · comment · 2026-07-06T23:51:14Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4898670571)

# nsys GPU-kernel trace — long-context prefill (the gating measurement)

**Build:** 9f18be76 (PR #41834), 1M ctx, TP4/EP4, packed FlashInfer SM120 prefill+decode, GB10.
**Captures:** two single-request prefills, `max_tokens=1`, unique prompts (no prefix-cache hit),
traced with `nsys --trace=cuda` wrapping the worker on rank0's GB10. Per-kernel GPU **durations
are exact** under nsys (overhead is CPU-launch-side); wall-clock inflated but irrelevant to the
% split. GPU stays **≈99.7% busy** in both — the fabric is not the wall here.

## Headline
**Long-context prefill is GPU-COMPUTE-bound (GPU ≈99.7% busy), NOT comms-bound. The dominant
kernel is the lightning-indexer's fp8 MQA-logits — and its share GROWS with context.**

## GPU-kernel time breakdown (rank0), two context sizes
| bucket                                      | ~200K-token req | ~536K-token req (window at higher accumulated ctx) |
|---------------------------------------------|:---------------:|:--------------------------------------------------:|
| **INDEXER — fp8 MQA-logits** (`_fp8_mqa_logits_kernel`) | **52.5%** | **59.3%** ↑ |
| MoE (Marlin W4A16 + block-mm + einsum + act)| 14.8%           | 11.4% ↓ |
| sparse-MLA prefill **attention** (`sparse_mla_prefill_mg_dual_kernel`) | 8.8% | 9.0% |
| INDEXER — top-k / compress (`topKPerRowPrefill<512>`) | 5.0%    | 5.7% |
| **COMMS** (NCCL all-reduce, RING_LL)        | 7.5%            | **5.4%** ↓ |
| MHC prenorm GEMM (TileLang)                 | 6.2%            | 5.1% |
| elementwise / copy / quant                  | 3.7%            | 2.9% |
| RoPE / RMSNorm                              | 1.5%            | 1.1% |
| **GPU busy**                                | **99.7%**       | **99.6%** |

**Combined lightning-indexer (MQA-logits + top-k + compress): 57.5% → 65.0%** as context grows.

## What this settles
1. **Your py-spy caveat was right to flag — but it isn't comms-inflation.** The "~50% MLA"
   py-spy bucket is the **indexer MQA-logits kernel** (52–59%), real GPU compute, not NCCL-wait.
   Comms is only 5–7% of GPU time and the GPU is 99.7% busy → prefill is genuinely
   compute-bound. (Decode stays the interconnect-latency-bound regime; prefill is not.)
2. **The scaling is the story.** From 200K→536K accumulated context the indexer's share *rises*
   (52.5%→59.3%) while MoE (14.8%→11.4%) and comms (7.5%→5.4%) *shrink*. That's the O(context)
   fingerprint: the indexer cost grows ~linearly with accumulated context, everything else is
   ~constant per token. This is exactly why single-request TTFT grows ~linearly with prompt
   length AND why parallel big prefills stall (each late chunk re-scans ≈full context).
3. **The actual sparse-MLA attention is only ~9%** — the packed FlashInfer SM120 prefill path
   (`PREFILL=1`) already keeps it cheap. The bottleneck is *upstream*, in the indexer.
4. **Highest-leverage target: `_fp8_mqa_logits_kernel`.** Is there a packed/FlashInfer or fused
   indexer path for **prefill**, analogous to the SM120 decode indexer? That single kernel is
   59% of a 536K prefill and rising — it moves single-request TTFT and the parallel stall
   together, far more than attention or MoE.
5. **NCCL tuning has low prefill upside** (comms 5–7%, falling with context). I applied multi-QP
   (`NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=4`) and am A/B-ing it, but the trace says the fabric isn't the
   prefill wall — it's the indexer. (Multi-QP may still help decode, which *is* comms-bound.)

Raw `.nsys-rep` traces (200K: 13 MB, 536K: 8 MB) available on request.

- jasl · comment · 2026-07-07T03:25:09Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4899817974)

@wingcomm This is a great trace — a per-kernel nsys split is exactly the measurement that settles the py-spy ambiguity, thank you. It lines up with what we've been seeing and sharpens it in one important way.

**On the attribution:** our earlier py-spy had bucketed that ~52% as "MLA," but your nsys resolves it correctly — it's the **lightning-indexer `_fp8_mqa_logits_kernel`**, and the actual sparse-MLA prefill attention (`sparse_mla_prefill_mg_dual_kernel`) is only ~9%. That matches our own kernel-level view: the indexer *scoring* is the O(N²) residual; the packed FlashInfer SM120 prefill path already keeps the attention itself cheap. Your O(context) scaling (52→59% as accumulated ctx grows, MoE/comms shrinking) is the N×N all-pairs signature — attention is ~O(N·d) per token, the indexer is the one that grows.

**On your headline ask — a packed/fused *prefill* indexer, analogous to the SM120 *decode* indexer:** we chased exactly this, and it looks like a hard floor recall-safely, so I'll save you the detour. The decode indexer packs because per step it scores 1×N; prefill is N×N. The sub-quadratic angles we tried all broke recall or were vacuous:

- interval/range-bound pruning → vacuous (≈0% pruned at the recall we need),
- cross-layer top-k reuse → no-go (top-512 overlap only ~38% across layers),
- pooled / block-sparse scoring → recall collapse (0.25–0.39; the pooled keys end up too cos-similar),
- MISA-dagger-style → only ~1.5×, and exact-only.

The kernel itself is already fp8 + tuned and **compute-bound (not bandwidth)** — fusing the top-k into it is only ~4%. So the realistic prefill wins there are constant-factor, not complexity; the O(N²) is inherent to top-k-selecting over the full context.

**On NCCL:** agreed, low prefill upside — comms at 5–7% and falling is consistent with what we see (prefill is compute-bound, the fabric isn't the wall). Decode is the other story: that *is* the interconnect-latency-bound regime for us on 2-node, so I'd be very interested in how your multi-QP (`NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=4`) A/B lands **on decode** specifically — if it moves decode, that's a real no-rebuild lever.

Would love the `.nsys-rep` traces (both sizes) if you don't mind sharing — the exact per-kernel timings are useful to diff against our own captures. Thanks again, this is high-signal.

The implementation there is cleaner than the vLLM fork's patch stack, and it's where our new work now lands. The vLLM fork stays available and maintained.

Same 2× DGX Spark GB10 pair, same fabric, same pinned llama-benchy, MTP2 + fp8 KV + prefix cache, C=1 × 3 runs. vLLM = our latest maintained fork head; TokenSpeed = `sm12x-stable` (torch 2.13, FlashInfer CUTLASS MXFP4 MoE):

| depth | ctx_pp t/s (TS / vLLM) | pp2048 (TS / vLLM) | tg128 peak (TS / vLLM) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8192  | **2057 / 1866** | 1404 / 1406 | 30.3 / 41.5 |
| 16384 | **2062 / 1825** | 1329 / 1354 | 28.7 / 41.3 |
| 32768 | **1979 / 1737** | 1149 / 1224 | 33.3 / 45.3 |

**Where TokenSpeed leads: cold-context prefill, by ~10-14%** — the dominant cost in the long-context / 1M scenarios several of you have raised (@wingcomm's 536K indexer-bound prefill, @brianmiller's 121K cold prefill). pp2048-at-depth is at parity (94-100%). **Decode is currently behind (~70-74%)** — the CUTLASS MoE that wins prefill has a weaker small-M decode GEMM; a hybrid path (CUTLASS prefill + Triton decode, single weight residency) is in progress to close it. Being upfront: if your workload is decode-heavy at low concurrency, the vLLM fork is still faster today.

Other wins worth noting:
- **KV capacity +25%** — 1.90M vs 1.52M tokens at `--max-model-len 131072`, same config.
- **Tool calling: 45/45 requests engine-clean, zero 500s** (the intermittent MTP + thinking + `tool_choice` 500s some of you hit are an upstream vLLM reasoning-boundary bug the fork inherits). Serve with `--grammar-backend xgrammar`.
- Long-gen GSM8K 0.96, zero illegal-memory-access.

## Build (GB10 2-node; RTX PRO 6000 single-node similar)

```bash
git clone -b sm12x-stable https://github.com/jasl/tokenspeed
sudo apt install python3.12-dev libssl-dev
uv venv --seed .venv-ts && source .venv-ts/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.13.0
pip install -r tokenspeed-kernel/python/requirements/cuda.txt
# skips the 10-30 min cold CUTLASS-MoE JIT on first boot:
pip install flashinfer-jit-cache==0.6.14+cu130 --index-url https://flashinfer.ai/whl/cu130
# GB10 = 121, RTX PRO 6000 = 120:
TOKENSPEED_CUDA_ARCH=121 pip install -e tokenspeed-kernel/python --no-build-isolation
pip install --no-deps nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.4    # REQUIRED on multi-node, see below
pip install -e tokenspeed-scheduler --no-build-isolation
pip install -e python
pip uninstall -y torchvision torchaudio           # unused; its torch-2.13 ABI trips transformers
```

Serve with `--moe-backend flashinfer_cutlass` (the prefill win; the registry otherwise auto-picks the Triton MoE) and `--grammar-backend xgrammar` for tool-calling.

Traps we hit so you don't have to:
- **`nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.4` is mandatory on multi-node host-staged RoCE.** 2.28.9 (torch's default), 2.29.7, and 2.30.7 all hit an NCCL graph-replay proxy-progress wedge that presents as serve hangs / late-wave request timeouts (this is likely behind several "2-node decode hang" reports in this thread). torch's dep re-resolves over manual pins on every editable install, so pin it with `--no-deps` **after** the kernel build. A minimal repro is headed to NVIDIA/nccl.
- `TOKENSPEED_CUDA_ARCH` must be set for the kernel build (no auto-detect → "no kernel image"); `rm -rf tokenspeed-kernel/python/objs` after changing it.
- `fast_hadamard_transform` must be built from the GitHub repo (`pip install --no-cache-dir --no-deps git+https://github.com/Dao-AILab/fast-hadamard-transform`) — the PyPI sdist is missing its `csrc/`.

Branches: `sm12x-stable` (validated) / `sm12x-preview` (gate-tested candidates) / `feat/sm12x-engine` (dev, may be unstable).

Benchy tables from your rigs are very welcome — especially the 8× RTX 5090 and 2× RTX PRO 6000 topologies we don't have here.

Most of the GB10 data here is 2-node TP=2, so adding a data point from the other end of the scale: **8× DGX Spark GB10 (SM121), TP=8, single-rail RoCE.** Built and cut over from `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260705` (`9f18be7|
6`, FlashInfer 0.6.13) → `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260711` (`b5c0d43b`, FlashInfer 0.6.14) with the recipe held identical across both:

### 1. Decode throughput — +57% at the TP=8 ceiling

Concurrent `/v1/completions`, short prompt, `min_tokens=128 ignore_eos temp=0`, idle cluster; aggregate = total completion tokens / wall time.

| concurrency | `9f18be76` (FI 0.6.13) | **`b5c0d43b`** (FI 0.6.14) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 56.4 tok/s | **64.0** | +13% |
| 4 | 116.6 | **176.4** | +51% |
| 8 | 154.9 | **253.6** | +64% |
| 16 | 166.0 | **261.1** | +57% |

The aggregate ceiling moved **~165 → ~261 tok/s**. Attributing it to **#47474** (`token_to_req_indices` caching) + the FI 0.6.14 decode path — it's the first thing in a while that broke the ceiling for us.

One TP=8-specific observation you won't see at TP=2: **decode is interconnect-latency-bound at this scale.** Aggregate plateaus by concurrency ~8 (8→16 adds almost nothing while per-stream halves), because every decode step is a
n 8-way all-reduce across 8 physical nodes — more concurrency amortizes the collective but can't shrink it. So the +57% is a real reduction in per-step overhead, but the wall above it is the fabric, not the kernel.

**Correctness held at 8-node scale** (`b5c0d43b`, GSM8K n=200, C=8, temp 0, max_tokens 3072): **acc 0.965 raw** (3 length-truncated → ~0.98 adjusted), **0 errors, 0% CJK** (no thinking-in-Chinese). In line with the promotion gat
e.

**Prefill unchanged**, as expected — a novel (prefix-cache-defeated) 100K-token prefill was 150s on both builds. #47474 is decode-only; our long-context prefill is bounded elsewhere (looks memory-bandwidth-bound on GB10 — happy
to share that separately, it's a longer story).

### 2. FI 0.6.14 costs KV pool at fixed util (−36%)

Same recipe, same `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.82`, the startup KV allocation dropped noticeably:

| build | FlashInfer | GPU KV cache size |
|---|---|---|
| `9f18be76` | 0.6.13 | **7,436,070 tokens** |
| `b5c0d43b` | 0.6.14 | **4,729,915 tokens** (−36%) |

Idle headroom also fell (~12 GB → ~9 GB avail at the same util). So FI 0.6.14 is holding more memory (buffers / jit-cache) at fixed util — a real capacity hit for long-context / high-concurrency serving where the KV pool is the
admission constraint. Recoverable by raising util, but headroom is tighter on this build so it needs load-testing. Flagging in case the extra footprint is unintended or tunable.

Net: on 8× GB10 TP=8, `b5c0d43b` is a clear decode win + correctness-neutral, with the one watch-item being the smaller KV pool. Thanks for the continued work on this path — glad to keep feeding scale data back.

<sub>Note: GPUs are clock-capped to 1800 MHz (peak-power management), so absolute tok/s may read a bit lower than uncapped rigs — but the 0.6.13→0.6.14 delta is measured under identical caps, so the comparison holds. We found de
code/prefill to be ~clock-insensitive here (interconnect/memory-bound), so the cap costs little.</sub>

- wingcomm · comment · 2026-07-13T04:04:11Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4954317153)

## Long-context prefill profiling on 8× GB10 TP=8 — looks memory-bandwidth-bound                                                                                                                                                    

Following up on our earlier decode/KV numbers with the prefill profiling we promised — sharing in case the GB10 scale data is useful, since long-context prefill keeps coming up in the thread. Same rig: **8× DGX Spark GB10 (SM121|
), TP=8, single-rail RoCE**, `b5c0d43b` (also confirmed on `9f18be76`).

### Symptom: novel prefill ~640 tok/s, linear in context
Prefix-cache-defeated (unique-nonce) single-stream prefill:

| context | latency | tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| 100K | 150 s | ~670 |
| 200K | 315 s | ~635 |
| 400K | 782 s | ~510 |

Roughly linear in tokens (slightly super-linear at the top), and unchanged across builds.

### Four measurements, all pointing to memory-bandwidth-bound

1. **Chunk-size independent** — `--max-num-batched-tokens` 16384 vs 32768 gave identical prefill times (100K = 150/151 s, 200K = 315 s both). If the per-chunk all-reduce dominated, doubling the chunk count would slow it → **not
collective/fabric-bound**, even at TP=8's 8-way reduce.
2. **Power/util** — during prefill every GPU sits at **96% util but only ~15 W** (idle 7 W; decode-under-load ~37–39 W). High-util + near-idle-power = SMs stalled on memory, not issuing FLOPs (and notably *less* power than decod
e).
3. **Clock-insensitive** — these run an 1800 MHz graphics-clock cap (hw max 3003) for peak-power. From a PDU-wattage sweep, long-context prefill **loses ~nothing** at 1800 vs 3003 (−40% clock) while peak draw drops ~30%. A 40% c
lock cut costing ~0 throughput is the memory-bound fingerprint.
4. **Bandwidth ceiling** — linear-in-context latency + (1)–(3) are consistent with being bounded by streaming/gathering KV through GB10's ~270 GB/s LPDDR5X, rather than ALUs or the interconnect.

### Observation
The memory-heavy actor in the DSv4 prefill is the **sparse-MLA indexer** (`sparse_attn_indexer` / `_fp8_mqa_logits`, the sm12x deep_gemm-fallback path you recently un-gated) — it scans the growing context for top-k selection, a
bandwidth-heavy scatter/gather, and on the fork it's the Triton path rather than a packed-FlashInfer one like the attention got. That matches the signature above, so at long context the indexer looks like the top cost rather tha
n the MoE GEMM — but that's inference from these four signals, not a kernel-level trace.

Two things we'd genuinely like to know:
- Does this match your profiles — is the indexer the dominant long-context prefill cost on the 2-node rig, or does MoE/attention lead?
- Is there a packed/FlashInfer indexer path on the roadmap (TokenSpeed or fork)? If the memory-bound read is right, that's the change we'd expect to move GB10 long-context prefill the most.

And an offer: happy to run whatever prefill profiling would help at **400K–1M context** — we have the scale to exercise the indexer where a 2-node rig can't reach.

- calper-ql · comment · 2026-07-13T08:16:42Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4955865536)

Hi, I've been running this PR's branch to serve DeepSeek-V4-Flash and hit a nasty prefix caching issue that I eventually traced back to a real bug, so posting it here in case it's useful.

**The symptom:** with spec decode on (so `use_eagle=True`), long-context sessions would randomly flip into a state where the prefix cache hit rate goes to exactly 0% and stays there. Every request re-prefills the whole prompt (~90s at 300k tokens on my setup). It's weirdly binary, either ~99.9% hits or 0%, never anything in between, and it flips without a restart. Took a while to convince myself the client wasn't mutating the prompt, it wasn't (verified byte-identical on the wire).

**The actual cause** is that the sliding window hit path and its block protection path disagree about how many contiguous blocks a hit needs. `SlidingWindowManager.find_longest_cache_hit` uses `_contiguous_blocks_for_hit(window, block_size, use_eagle)`, which adds +1 under eagle since the last matched block gets dropped. For `sliding_window=128` / `block_size=64` that's **3** contiguous blocks. But `SlidingWindowMLAManager.cache_blocks` computes its protection width inline as `cdiv(self.sliding_window - 1, self.block_size)` without the eagle +1, so it only pins **2**. The third block sits there evictable, and as soon as some other request churns the pool it gets evicted. Then the SWA probe returns 0, and because the hybrid coordinator takes the min across groups at the boundary, one missing SWA block zeroes the entire hit. Hence the all-or-nothing behavior.

**Fix** is one line, just make `cache_blocks` use the same helper the hit path uses:

```python
contiguous_blocks = self._contiguous_blocks_for_hit(
    self.sliding_window, self.block_size, self.use_eagle
)
```

Non-eagle behavior is unchanged.

**Verified** with a reproducer (prime 300k ctx, interpose one unrelated request to churn the pool, resend a byte-identical extension): before the fix the extension gets 0% hits and recomputes all 300k tokens, after it's 100% with 131 tokens computed, 0.6s instead of ~90s.

One more thing I noticed while digging: the fallback in `kv_cache_coordinator.py` (~L102) marks *all* KV groups as eagle groups, which is what routes the SWA group onto the eagle path here in the first place. The one-liner above fixes the inconsistency either way, but that fallback might deserve a look too.

- wingcomm · comment · 2026-07-15T07:10:20Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4977856054)

# P/D disaggregation data on 8× GB10 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SM120)

Sharing some prefill/decode disaggregation numbers from an 8× GB10 setup, since the NIXL P/D work (#46694, #45880) is landing. Short version: for a **prefill-bound long-context workload**, disagg was a net regression vs monolithic TP=8 on this hardware, and the reason is specific to GB10 — prefill throughput doesn't scale with TP, so partitioning nodes away from the shared pool just lowers peak prefill capacity without buying anything.

## Setup

- **8× GB10**, RDMA fabric between nodes.
- Build: `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260713` (`cfddacb`), FlashInfer 0.6.14, packed SM120 sparse-MLA decode **and** prefill, MTP (k=2).
- Monolithic config: TP=8, `max_model_len=1M`, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.82`, `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`.
- Disagg config: **1× prefill engine (TP=4) + 1× decode engine (TP=4)**, `NixlConnector` pull mode over RDMA, reference `toy_proxy_server.py`. Only one prefiller instance is possible here — the model needs TP≥4 to fit, so the decode side can't drop below 4 nodes, which leaves exactly 4 for prefill.
- Workload: agentic / linear-thread, 100–500K context, high prefix-cache hit rate (~91% by tokens), bursty arrivals. The pain is the cold-miss tail — genuinely new large contexts.

## Finding 1 — prefill does not scale TP=4 → TP=8

Same large (~novel) prefill, measured both ways:

| Topology | Prefill wall-clock |
|---|---|
| TP=4 (disagg prefill engine) | **274.6 s** |
| TP=8 (monolithic) | **315 s** |

TP=8 was ~13% **slower** for a single big prefill. On this fabric the added 8-way collective/coordination cost roughly cancels the extra compute — prefill here is bandwidth- and coordination-bound, not cleanly TP-parallel. (Single-shot comparison, same prompt; not a full sweep — but the direction was consistent across our runs.) This matches the long-context-prefill memory-bandwidth constraint noted earlier in the thread.

**Consequence for disagg:** you can't cheaply add prefill throughput by adding prefill ranks. So splitting 8 nodes into 4+4 halves the prefill parallelism you had under TP=8 while the coordination wall stays put.

## Finding 2 — the static partition strands capacity under prefill-bound load

Snapshot under production traffic, disagg config:

- **Prefill engine: 4 running + 6 waiting, KV ~90%** — saturated.
- **Decode engine: 0 running, ~0% util, ~7 W (idle floor)** — stranded.

When the workload is prefill-bound, the 4 decode nodes can't be borrowed for prefill — they sit idle while the prefill side is backlogged. Monolithic TP=8 puts all 8 nodes on whichever phase is the current bottleneck, so it never strands half the cluster. Decode *isolation* works as designed (in-flight decodes are unaffected by prefill); it just provides no benefit when prefill is the wall and nothing is getting through to fill the decode pool.

(Prefill saturation from big cold prefills monopolizing the scheduler is a **separate, still-open problem** we see on monolithic TP=8 too — it isn't caused by the split and isn't evidence either way. It's noted here only to explain why the decode pool sat idle.)

## Takeaway

For **prefill-bound, long-context** traffic on GB10-class hardware, P/D disagg with a fixed node budget is counterproductive: prefill's lack of TP scaling means the shared monolithic pool (all nodes available to whichever phase needs them, plus one large prefix-cache) beats a static 4+4 partition. Disagg would need either (a) more prefill parallelism than TP scaling can deliver here, or (b) a decode-bound workload, to pay off.

Where disagg *might* still help on this hardware: decode-heavy / high-concurrency serving where the decode pool would actually stay saturated, or multi-prefiller setups on larger node counts where prefill capacity can grow horizontally rather than via TP. Neither applies to the single-big-prefill, linear-thread case.

Happy to share more detail (NIXL handshake, proxy config, per-phase KV pool sizes) if useful for the P/D work.

- jasl · comment · 2026-07-15T09:28:37Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-4979039253)

Really useful data. It's worth nailing down whether the TP=8 penalty is the RoCE floor or something reclaimable, because the two point at opposite fixes. Here's how I'd settle it cheapest-first — happy to share our harness (we ran this exact ladder to crack the analogous *decode* wall on the same CRS804 fabric, and it turned out host-side, not the all-reduce).

**Why I'd bet implementation a priori.** At 100–500K, the DSv4 prefill wall is dominated by O(N·topk) sparse-attn/indexer *compute*, not AR bytes — and compute should roughly **halve** TP4→8. For TP=8 to be *slower*, some rank-growing term has to beat that ~2× compute saving. The ring null-model has AR bytes/rank growing only 1.5·S→1.75·S (+16.7%), and that's +16.7% of the AR *fraction* of the wall, not the whole wall. So either AR is a far bigger fraction than the physics suggests (→ hardware), or the culprit is **indexer/MLA not sharding + host dispatch** (→ ours).

**The one-shot test — it can outright refute hardware.** Bare `all_reduce_perf` at the **real prefill AR size** `S = chunk_tokens × hidden × 2B` (bf16), not the decode-heartbeat size, across 4 real nodes then all 8, with the serve's exact `NCCL_*` env, **nccl 2.30.4**, warmup discarded. `ΔAR_bench = time/op × (AR count per prefill)`, TP=8 − TP=4. A few seconds while the wall grew ~40s → the fabric physically can't carry it → **implementation**. ≈40s at ~22.6 GB/s with no headroom → **hardware**, confirm in-window.

**The trap that voids most attempts:** reason **in-window**, never on the run average (~1 GB/s over a 315s prefill always looks idle and proves nothing). Then `nsys` one warm chunk (does the actual per-AR hit the bench ceiling, back-to-back? does compute-kernel time actually **halve** 4→8? if not → indexer/MLA not sharding, and no NCCL knob helps), sweep `NCCL_ALGO=Tree` vs `Ring` + proto + channels as the reclaim lever, and if you can patch one line, a same-shape no-op AR stub re-timed at TP=8 exonerates the fabric outright. Two gotchas that'll waste a day: confirm the dominant collective is **AllReduce, not all-to-all** (if MoE is EP-sharded across the 8 the byte math is different and worse), and pin **nccl 2.30.4** — 2.30.7 proxy-thread death on the Spark host-staged RoCE transport gives a false-catastrophic fabric reading.

My money's on indexer/MLA-not-sharding + host dispatch over the RoCE floor, but the bare bench settles it in one run. And yes — the per-phase KV-pool sizes you offered would be great; they feed straight into our long-context capacity work.

@jasl We traced and fixed an MTP2 + native CPU KV offload failure that affects this branch's DeepSeek V4 hybrid SWA geometry.

Standalone upstream PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48911

The store-pruning predicate had two mismatches with lookup:

1. EAGLE/MTP lookup requires `sliding_window_tail + 1` chunks before popping the volatile draft tail, but store retained only `tail`.
2. Store compared against the configured full alignment length, so a final partial segment (48-of-64 in our trace) stored none of its reachable tail.

The fixed image restored 18,688/18,877 tokens on the exact proof and 99,840/100,006 tokens on a practical 100K replay (23.56s cold -> 0.61s first CPU hit -> 0.40s second), while MTP2 decode stayed ~190 tok/s and full 1M admission remained intact.

The PR is based on current upstream main after the chunk terminology refactor. For this branch, the accepted equivalent source commit is `7bf379f7ff3f64607a345e9e67fc2578121a7d31`; cherry-picking the upstream PR commit is preferable once #48911 settles because it includes current-main direct regressions for both Eagle `tail+1` and partial segments.

- coltonottley · comment · 2026-07-19T15:41:04Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-5016327054)

@jasl — you previously noted that CPU KV offload was not a supported feature of the SM12x branch. We kept investigating it because host-RAM prefix retention is unusually valuable for long-lived agent workloads.

The largest result is storage efficiency. The original TP=2 CPU representation consumed roughly 187–195 KiB of server RAM per unique logical token. The final shared canonical TP1 representation uses approximately 4.1 KiB per unique token—about a 40× improvement end to end.

That changes CPU offload from a mechanism demonstration into a practical serving feature:

- approximately 16.7 million unique tokens retained in a 64 GiB CPU tier;
- DeepSeek V4 Flash with MTP2, FP8 KV, and full 1M-token context preserved;
- approximately 190 output tok/s decode on 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs;
- exact 100K-token histories restored from CPU RAM in roughly 0.4–0.6 seconds after GPU eviction;
- validated on two independent TP=2 hosts, each with 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, plus a TP=4 qualification;
- natural agent traffic is already producing real external-cache reuse: 29.7% external hit rate on one host and 8.7% on another.

The roughly 40× improvement came from two architectural changes:

1. compact fixed-page scatter storage removed roughly 19× packing amplification in DeepSeek V4's heterogeneous hybrid cache layout;
2. one shared canonical TP1 CPU payload removed the remaining 2× duplicate storage across TP ranks.

The 19× component is specific to heterogeneous hybrid layouts like DeepSeek V4 rather than ordinary uniform transformer KV caches. The rank-deduplication component is more broadly useful for replicated MLA.

The production implementation also includes fragmentation-proof allocation, owner-scoped shared-memory lifecycle and guarded orphan recovery, reset/concurrency handling, metrics, and restart qualification.

We intentionally did not dump the downstream implementation into your branch while upstream CPU-offload code was changing. We did not want to hand you an unreviewed maintenance fork.

Would you be interested in collaborating on making this an optional, disabled-by-default CPU-offload capability for the SM12x branch?

We can carry the current-branch port, focused regressions, and TP=2/TP=4 hardware qualification. We would also align it with the existing shared CPU-primary and canonical-mapping work rather than create competing architecture.

No obligation to own the feature alone—we're offering to carry the implementation and hardware-validation work with you.

- kelnei · comment · 2026-08-01T03:43:51Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-5149637969)

### DSpark on DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731: `num_speculative_tokens=7` silently collapses draft acceptance to ~4%. Should the validator require `== dspark_block_size`?

First off, thanks for this branch, it's what makes DSV4-Flash usable on our hardware at all.

**Setup:** 2x DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121), TP2 via Ray across nodes, this PR (head `d64074e`) applied onto its merge-base (`7f599d7`, main @ 2026-07-27), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, MoE backend auto-selects Marlin MXFP4. Model is the official `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` checkpoint (`dspark_block_size: 5`).

**Symptom:** with the model card's recommended spec config

```json
{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 7, "draft_sample_method": "greedy"}
```

draft acceptance is catastrophically low on ordinary prose, and not just at the two positions past the block size: **all positions collapse**.

```
SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.31, Accepted throughput: 13.40 tokens/s,
Drafted throughput: 302.37 tokens/s, Per-position acceptance rate:
0.181, 0.067, 0.039, 0.014, 0.009, 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 4.4%
```

The same config with `num_speculative_tokens: 5` is healthy:

```
SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 2.74, Per-position acceptance rate:
0.579, 0.447, 0.316, 0.237, 0.158, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 34.7%
```

(pos-0 ranges 0.58-0.78 across runs; single-stream decode goes ~26 to ~40 tok/s on our setup.)

**What we ruled out** (nst was the only variable that mattered, across 14 boots):

- greedy vs `draft_sample_method: probabilistic`: identical collapse at nst=7
- prefix caching on/off: no change
- `--enforce-eager` vs full cudagraphs: no change
- disabling each `dspark_*` accel toggle (`dspark_materialized_attention`, `dspark_triton_attention`, `dspark_triton_qkv_postprocess`, `dspark_triton_context_kv_store`, `dspark_markov_inplace_add`, `dspark_fused_markov_sampler`, `dspark_fused_o_proj_quant`, `dspark_fused_shared_experts_quant`) individually and all together: all fine at nst=5, none rescue nst=7
- weight loading: all 99 draft params load (verified the name mapping against the checkpoint index), aux layers picked up from `dspark_target_layer_ids` (40, 41, 42) correctly

**Why this is worth a guard:** the current `SpeculativeConfig` validator enforces `num_speculative_tokens >= dspark_block_size` and its error message actively recommends the broken value:

> DSpark requires num_speculative_tokens >= dspark_block_size (5); got 3. Smaller values produce incorrect output. Use num_speculative_tokens=5 or larger (e.g. 7).

Since the drafter emits exactly one block of 5 per pass (multi-block drafting doesn't appear to be implemented), everything above 5 seems to misalign the whole proposal. Both this message and the HF model card steer users straight into a config that looks alive (positions 0-4 get ~4% noise-level acceptance, output text stays correct) but destroys spec-decode throughput. Unless multi-block drafting is intended to work here, it'd save users a lot of debugging if the validator required `num_speculative_tokens == dspark_block_size` (or clamped with a warning).

One observation for anyone else chasing this: acceptance probes on highly predictable text (counting, repeated sequences) are misleading for DSpark. The Markov head alone gets 68-98% acceptance on bigram-predictable output even when nst=7 has the neural draft path fully degraded. Test on prose.

Happy to provide full boot logs or run further tests on sm_121 if useful.

- mzzhome-ai · comment · 2026-08-01T12:08:35Z · [source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-5151353498)

### DSpark speculative decoding on 4x DGX Spark (GB10, sm121): two distinct failures, one per attention backend

Reporting from a configuration that I think is not represented yet in this thread: **four DGX Spark nodes, one GB10 each, TP=4 with expert parallelism, connected over RoCE/InfiniBand** (`--distributed-executor-backend mp`, `--nnodes 4`). Everything below is on the **official BF16/FP8 checkpoint**, not an NVFP4 conversion.

**Environment**

- 4x NVIDIA GB10 (sm121), 128 GB unified memory per node, ConnectX-7 RoCE
- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev191+gaef9bd1e9.d20260731` (community image `eugr/spark-vllm:nightly-20260731`)
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, official weights
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --block-size 256 --max-model-len 1000000 --max-num-seqs 4 --enable-expert-parallel --enable-prefix-caching`
- `num_speculative_tokens: 5`, matching `dspark_block_size: 5` from the model config

**Baseline: without `--speculative-config` everything works.** The model loads (41.5 GiB per node), allocates KV cache, serves requests, tool calling and the reasoning parser both behave correctly. The failures below appear only when the DSpark draft is enabled.

---

#### Case 1 — default attention backend (resolves to `DeepseekV4FlashInferSM120Attention`)

```
--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
```

```
tvm.error.InternalError: Check failed: num_tokens > 64 (5 vs. 64) :
Decode (num_tokens <= 64) must go through sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv3_2
or sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv4; got num_tokens=5
```

Path: `kernel_warmup` → `deepseek_v4_sparse_mla_attention_warmup` → `_deepseek_v4_sparse_mla_decode_autotune` → `run_mixed_prefill_decode_warmup` → `speculator.propose` → `dspark/speculator.py::_generate_draft` → `nvidia/flashinfer_sparse.py::_forward_decode` → `flashinfer_trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4` → `_sparse_mla_sm120_paged_attention` → `sparse_mla_sm120.cu:261`.

The draft submits K tokens, which is always well under 64, so the paged kernel rejects it. `--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune` does not help: it governs the general FlashInfer autotuner, while `deepseek_v4_sparse_mla_attention_warmup` runs regardless.

#### Case 2 — `--attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV4`

Per `_select_dsv4_attn_cls` in `models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/model.py`, this selects `DeepseekV4FlashMLAAttention` with no device-capability gate, so it is reachable on sm121. It does move execution off the FlashInfer path — the `num_tokens > 64` error disappears — but fails later:

```
AssertionError: swa_metadata missing tile_sched entry for compress_ratio=1;
DeepseekSparseSWAMetadataBuilder.build_tile_scheduler did not allocate one
for this layer type.
```

Path: same warmup, then `nvidia/flashmla.py::forward_mqa` → `_forward_decode` (line 218).

Note that `compress_ratio=1` does not appear in the model's `compress_ratios` array, whose values are `0`, `4` and `128`. It looks like the draft layers (`dspark_target_layer_ids: [40, 41, 42]`) end up on a default the SWA tile scheduler does not allocate for.

---

Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware if that is useful — a four-node GB10 cluster over RoCE is awkward to come by, and I am glad to test patches on it.

I am running @jasl's branch on the exact same setup without issues. This is my configuration:

```
build_args:
  - --vllm-repo
  - https://github.com/jasl/vllm.git
  - --vllm-ref
  - d64074e6f07250f6cd072861aa3c389a929befb9
  - --rebuild-vllm
  - --rebuild-flashinfer
  - --deepgemm-ref
  - nv_dev
  
defaults:
  port: 8000
  host: 0.0.0.0
  tensor_parallel: 4
  gpu_memory_utilization: 0.9   # KV rate is ~63k tok/GiB (MLA fp8, measured: 12.84GiB=810k tok at 0.80). 0.78 -> ~11GiB KV = ~660k token pool, enough for 500k context (1.3x concurrency), with more RAM buffer -> less swap.
  max_model_len: 1048576
  block_size: 256
  max_num_seqs: 10
  max_num_batched_tokens: 4096
  num_speculative_tokens: 7   # design point: vendor dspark_block_size=5 (head trained for blocks of 5); 5 beat 4 on eff t/s; 6 predicted flat/negative (pos-6 accept ~0.5 for a full extra Markov step).
  served_model_name: deepseek-v4-flash

env:
  TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST: 12.1a
  VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN: 1
  VLLM_TRITON_MLA_SPARSE: 1
  VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_DECODE: 1
  VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_PREFILL: 1
  # DeepGEMM scale-layout JIT currently fails on GB10 with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_IMAGE.
  VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM: 0
  VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM: 1
  VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM_E8M0: 0
  DG_JIT_USE_NVRTC: "0"
  VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN: "1"
  VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH: "0"
  VLLM_MEMORY_PROFILER_ESTIMATE_CUDAGRAPHS: "0"   # don't reserve FULL-cudagraph memory in the profiler (it ate ~99% of budget -> 0.61GiB KV). KV gets the budget; capture uses on-top headroom. Fork uses this.
  PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF: "expandable_segments:True"   # reduce unified-memory fragmentation -> a bit more usable for KV. Fork uses this.
  VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER: "1"   # spec-decode hygiene (tonyd2wild garble-fix); takes effect on next relaunch.
  VLLM_DSPARK_FORWARD_CUDAGRAPH: "1"
  VLLM_DSPARK_FORWARD_CUDAGRAPH_ALLOW_TP: "1"
  
command: |
  vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \
      --host {host} \
      --port {port} \
      --override-generation-config '{{"top_p":0.95}}' \
      --async-scheduling \
      --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4 \
      --block-size {block_size} \
      --compilation-config '{{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE","custom_ops":["all"],"cudagraph_capture_sizes":[6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48]}}' \
      --default-chat-template-kwargs.reasoning_effort max \
      --default-chat-template-kwargs.thinking true \
      --distributed-executor-backend ray \
      --enable-auto-tool-choice \
      --enable-chunked-prefill \
      --enable-flashinfer-autotune \
      --enable-prefix-caching \
      --gpu-memory-utilization {gpu_memory_utilization} \
      --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
      --load-format instanttensor \
      --max-cudagraph-capture-size 48 \
      --max-model-len {max_model_len} \
      --max-num-batched-tokens {max_num_batched_tokens} \
      --max-num-seqs {max_num_seqs} \
      --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \
      --served-model-name {served_model_name} \
      --speculative-config '{{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":{num_speculative_tokens},"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}}' \
      --tensor-parallel-size {tensor_parallel} \
      --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \
      --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \
      --trust-remote-code

## Update 2026-08-02 — `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, 234 upstream commits, DSpark fixes

New validated head: tag **`sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260802`** (`9a94c54292`), 234 upstream commits absorbed, level with `upstream/main` as of 2026-08-02.

@kelnei @mzzhome-ai @allenh1 — this reworks the DSpark path you all reported on, so the
details below are aimed at your configurations. Short version: **none of the three failures
reproduce on this head**, but chasing them turned up two real defects that are now fixed,
plus a model-side change that removes MTP as an option.

### The three reports, re-tested on this head

Everything below is on `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, 2x GB10 (sm_121) TP=2 unless noted.

| Report | Result here |
| --- | --- |

Your diagnosis was right; `nst=7` is now rejected at startup. |

Serve came up, 56.9 GiB / 8,366,891 token KV. |
